title: Infrastructure as Code: Vendor-Specific Examples
overview: IaC defines infrastructure in versioned files rather than manual clicks. Compare provisioning, configuration and orchestration, then apply them to AWS serverless, Azure microservices, a GCP pipeline and multi-cloud Kubernetes. GitOps keeps cluster desired state in Git and synchronises it through automation.
big_ideas: IaC = provisioning and managing infrastructure through scripts or config files instead of manual configuration.
IaC automates repeatable environments and records reviewed changes; reverting code still requires a safe infrastructure update.
IaC reference architecture has three components: infrastructure provisioning, configuration management, orchestration.
Best practices: modular design, environment segmentation (Dev/Test/Prod), and state management.
Vendor-native tools (AWS SAM/CloudFormation, Azure Bicep/ARM) suit a single cloud; Terraform is the cross-cloud tool.
Kubernetes IaC is declarative (desired state in YAML/JSON), stored in Git, and applied by GitOps automation with Git as the source of truth.

sections.title: IaC concepts and reference architecture
sections.summary: What IaC is, its benefits and tools, the components and best practices of an IaC reference architecture, and the three example architectures.
notes: **IaC defines repeatable environments in versioned files.** Tools automate setup, reduce manual differences and record changes. Reuse modules while deliberately parameterising differences such as production size, access and region.

**Reference architecture has three components:** infrastructure provisioning (create VMs, containers, databases, networks), configuration management (software configured as intended, e.g. Ansible, Chef) and orchestration (workflows, deployments, scaling, e.g. Kubernetes, Terraform).

**Three best practices:** modular design (reusable networking/compute modules), environment segmentation (isolated Dev, Test, Prod) and state management (track current infrastructure for smoother updates).

**Tool choice follows scope:** native tools (CloudFormation/SAM, Bicep, the GCP tooling illustrated in the lecture) for one cloud; Terraform for cross-cloud; Helm, Kustomize, Argo CD for Kubernetes. The examples are a serverless AWS app, microservices on Azure AKS, an event-driven GCP pipeline and multiple Kubernetes clusters across clouds.

terms.def: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled files that tools apply automatically.
Keeping software on provisioned machines in the intended configuration (e.g. Ansible, Chef).
Coordinating deployments, workflows and scaling across many resources (e.g. Kubernetes, Terraform).
Tracking what infrastructure currently exists so updates and scaling go smoothly.
Keeping Dev, Test and Prod isolated for safer deployments.

check.q: A change that passed in test fails in production, and the team finds production was hand-edited months ago. How would IaC have prevented this, and does it mean test must be identical to production?
check.a: If the same reviewed modules build every environment and all changes go through code, the hand edit could not have drifted unnoticed, and version history would show what changed. It does not require identical environments: size, access and region should be explicit parameters. Drift only stays away if nobody makes manual changes outside the code.

check.q: VMs and databases are created correctly from templates, but an app fails because a library version on the VMs differs from the one expected. Which IaC component is missing, and which would not help?
check.a: Configuration management, which makes sure the software on provisioned resources is set up as intended. Provisioning only created the resources correctly, and orchestration manages deployment workflows and scaling, so neither addresses what is installed on the VMs. Baking the dependency into an immutable image is another way to solve it.

check.q: Three product teams each copy and edit the same 800-line network template, and a security fix had to be made in three places. Which IaC best practices would you apply?
check.a: Modular design: extract a reusable, versioned networking module that every team consumes with its own parameters, so a fix is made once and rolled out. Add environment segmentation so Dev, Test and Prod are isolated, and state management so each apply knows the current infrastructure. The trade-off is that changes to a shared module need versioning and testing, because one change now affects every team.

check.q: Two engineers run applies against the same environment at the same time and resources end up duplicated. Which best practice was missing, and why does it matter?
check.a: State management: the tooling needs one tracked record of the current infrastructure, kept in one shared place that every apply reads and updates. Without it, each apply works from a different view of reality, and updates or scaling create duplicates or destroy resources unexpectedly.

sections.title: Vendor-native IaC: AWS SAM and Azure Bicep
sections.summary: Two worked examples using each provider's own IaC tooling: a serverless web app on AWS and a containerised microservices app on Azure.
notes: **Native templates describe the whole solution, not just compute.** The AWS serverless app (Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, S3 for static content) is defined in a SAM template with permissions and CloudWatch logging; deploy with sam build and sam deploy.

**The Azure microservices app (AKS, Cosmos DB, VNet with Private Endpoints, Application Gateway with WAF) is defined in Bicep/ARM,** including Azure Monitor logging and role assignments so AKS reaches Cosmos DB securely; deploy with az deployment group create.
**Security and observability are part of the template,** so they are deployed identically every time rather than bolted on manually.
**SAM/CloudFormation vs Bicep/ARM:** same declarative idea on different clouds, both single-provider; choose native tools when everything lives on one provider and Terraform when it spans clouds.

terms.def: Serverless Application Model: a simplified way to define serverless apps, used with CloudFormation.
AWS's native IaC service that provisions resources from YAML/JSON templates.
Azure's concise IaC language for deploying Azure resources; the alternative to ARM templates.
Azure Resource Manager template, Azure's native JSON IaC format.
Web Application Firewall: filters malicious HTTP traffic in front of an app.

check.q: In one project, the function, API and table are defined in the IaC template, but permissions and logging are configured by hand in the console afterwards. What is the risk?
check.a: The security and observability settings are not versioned, so a redeploy or a new environment can come up without them, or with different permissions. The lecture's serverless template defines permissions and logging alongside the resources so they deploy the same way every time. The cost is a larger template that must be reviewed carefully.

check.q: A containerised app reaches its database over a public endpoint protected by IP firewall rules. A reviewer asks for private endpoints in the virtual network and a role assignment for the cluster instead. What does each change gain, and what does it cost?
check.a: A private endpoint keeps database traffic on the private network, so the database is not exposed to the internet at all; firewall rules on a public endpoint can be misconfigured or bypassed by a compromised allowed address. A role assignment grants the cluster identity-based access, so no secret has to be stored and rotated. The costs are more network design and harder access for tools outside the network.

check.q: A company is all-in on one cloud and is choosing between that provider's native declarative IaC and Terraform. What should decide it?
check.a: If everything lives on one provider, native tools are designed for its services and model them directly, which favours them. Terraform is the better choice if the company expects to span clouds or wants one language and workflow across providers. The trade-off is depth on one cloud versus portability of skills and tooling.

sections.title: Terraform, multi-cloud and Kubernetes GitOps
sections.summary: Terraform examples for a GCP event-driven pipeline and a multi-cloud Kubernetes deployment, then Kubernetes IaC principles: declarative config, version control and GitOps.
notes: **Terraform is the cross-cloud choice.** One language and workflow with a provider per platform; the GCP event-driven pipeline (Pub/Sub, Cloud Functions or Cloud Run, BigQuery, monitoring) is provisioned this way, with IAM set per component for least privilege.

**Multi-cloud Kubernetes means separate clusters with common provisioning.** Terraform modules create EKS, AKS and GKE. Connectivity, federated identity, workload placement, scaling and logging need additional configuration; GitOps can synchronise workload definitions. The example commands initialise providers and apply the declared resources.
**Kubernetes IaC is declarative:** YAML/JSON describe desired state rather than imperative steps, and live in Git for traceability, collaboration and rollback.

**GitOps separates desired state from live state.** Review a Git change, let automation synchronise the cluster, then check convergence. Reverting a commit changes desired state; successful recovery still depends on compatible application versions, schemas and persistent data.

terms.def: Cloud-agnostic IaC tool that uses a provider per platform to provision resources across clouds.
Plugin that lets Terraform manage a specific platform such as AWS, Azure or Google.
Grant each component only the permissions it needs.
You describe the desired end state and the tool works out how to reach it, versus imperative step-by-step commands.
Operating model where Git holds the desired state and automation (e.g. Argo CD) applies it to clusters.

check.q: One Terraform configuration creates clusters on three providers. A manager says 'we now have one cross-cloud cluster'. Is that right?
check.a: No. It provisions separate clusters with a common tool and workflow. Connectivity between them, federated identity, workload placement, scaling and logging still have to be designed and configured, and GitOps can keep workload definitions in sync. A common tool reduces the provisioning work but does not make the clusters one system.

check.q: An operator scales a Deployment by hand with a command during an incident. Ten minutes later it is back to its old size. Why, and what should they have done?
check.a: Under GitOps the declared state in Git is the source of truth, and the sync tool reconciled the live cluster back to it. The change should be made as a reviewed Git commit, or reconciliation paused deliberately during the incident with the fix committed afterwards. This is the declarative model working as intended: imperative changes do not last.

check.q: A bad release is reverted in Git and the cluster syncs, but the app still fails. What does a Git rollback not undo?
check.a: Reverting a commit restores the desired configuration, but not persistent data or a database schema migration the new version already applied. If the old version can't read the new schema, the rollback fails. Plan backward-compatible schema changes or a data recovery step, and check that the cluster has actually converged before declaring recovery.

check.q: In an event-driven pipeline, every component is provisioned with a single broad service identity because it was quicker. What would you change in the IaC, and why there?
check.a: Give each component its own identity with only the permissions it needs, for example publish-only for the producer and write-only to the analytics table for the processor. Defining this in IaC applies the least-privilege policy the same way every time and keeps it under review. The cost is more identities and policies to manage, but a compromised component can no longer reach everything.

steps.label: Edit YAML
steps.detail: Resources are described declaratively as YAML/JSON representing the desired state.

steps.label: Git commit / PR
steps.detail: Git is the source of truth; gives traceability, collaboration and rollback.

steps.label: Argo CD
steps.detail: Automation synchronises desired state from Git and reports whether applying it succeeded.

steps.label: Kubernetes cluster
steps.detail: Controllers reconcile workloads to the applied specifications. Reverting Git does not restore persistent application data.

exam_angles.q: A company's Dev, Test and Prod environments keep drifting apart, two engineers sometimes apply changes at the same time, and 30% of production deployments fail. Propose an IaC-based remedy and say what discipline it requires from the team.
exam_angles.a: Define all infrastructure in reusable, versioned modules in Git, with each environment as a separate, isolated set of parameters (environment segmentation). Keep one shared, tracked state so concurrent applies work from the same view, and apply only through a pipeline after review. Configuration management or immutable images keep the software consistent too. It only works if nobody changes infrastructure by hand; incident fixes must also go through code.

exam_angles.q: Choose IaC tooling for (a) a 5-person startup building only on one provider's serverless services and (b) an enterprise running Kubernetes on three providers. Justify each, and say what each choice gives up.
exam_angles.a: (a) The provider's native declarative IaC: it is designed for that cloud's services and can define functions, APIs, tables, permissions and logging in one template. It gives up portability if the startup later spans clouds. (b) Terraform with a provider per cloud and reusable cluster modules, plus GitOps for the workloads: one language and workflow across clouds. It gives up some native depth, and connectivity and federated identity still have to be designed separately.

exam_angles.q: Design the IaC for an event-driven pipeline: messages are ingested, processed by functions and written to an analytics store. A security review requires that a compromised processor cannot read or delete other data. Explain the security decisions in the template.
exam_angles.a: Provision the topic, subscription, function and analytics tables in one declarative configuration, with monitoring and logging defined alongside. Give each component its own identity: the processor can only consume from its subscription and write to its table. Because the IaC defines these permissions, they are reviewed and applied the same way in every environment. The trade-off is more identities to manage, in exchange for a much smaller blast radius.

exam_angles.q: A team uses GitOps for its Kubernetes platform. A release that adds a database column fails, and an engineer proposes 'just revert the commit'. Explain what GitOps gives here and what the revert will and will not fix.
exam_angles.a: GitOps keeps the declared state in Git and lets automation reconcile the cluster to it, which gives traceability, review and a quick way back to the previous configuration. Reverting restores the old Deployment, but the schema change has already been applied. If the old version can't work with the new column, the app still fails. Use backward-compatible migrations or a data recovery step, and verify convergence before calling it fixed.

exam_angles.q: A reviewer compares two IaC designs for a containerised app and its database. Design A exposes the database on a public endpoint with IP allow-lists and stores a database password in the cluster. Design B places the database behind a private endpoint in the virtual network, puts a web application firewall at the edge, and grants the cluster a role assignment. Which would you approve, and what does B cost?
exam_angles.a: Approve B. The private endpoint removes public exposure of the database, the WAF filters malicious traffic at the edge, and identity-based role assignment removes a long-lived secret that could leak. Defining all of this in the template means the same controls are present in every environment. B costs more network design, and tools outside the network can't reach the database without a controlled path.
